title: Be Human
author: John Mark Reynolds
source: Canon: John Mark N. Reynolds (johnmarkreynolds.substack.com), November 9, 2026
summary: John Mark Reynolds reads the opening line of Homer's Odyssey as a lesson in what it means to be human. He notes that the poet hesitates to name the hero, calling him the man of many ways, and contrasts that resourceful figure with the proud man of one way who runs at every wall. Odysseus is worth following because he fails yet finds another way and never confuses the means with the end. Reynolds argues that Odysseus first mistakes his task for staying alive, then learns through sorrow that he must get home, preferring wife and home to Calypso's easy paradise. He applies this to ministries, schools and colleges, which he says too often behave as if the goal were to do business rather than to find a home fit for human beings. The short essay is a typical example of his habit of drawing formation lessons from the primary texts of the classical tradition.
points: Odysseus is the man of many ways, who answers No way with New way, in contrast to the narcissist with only one way.
The hero worth following fails but finds a way and never confuses the means with the end.
Odysseus errs by treating survival as his job, and Calypso's island shows that godlike ease is miserable for a mortal who wants home.
Reynolds charges that schools and ministries run as if their goal is doing business, when every task should be homeward bound.
Great texts are read here as pedagogy: the Odyssey is used to teach what a human being is for.
quotes: The hero, the man worth following, will fail, but will find a way. He never confuses the means with the end.
He is the man who hears: “No way!” and says: “New way!” The stubborn man, the narcissist, hears “no way” and bulls ahead.
Put a wall in his way and the proud man will try to run through the wall. Sometimes this works and his pride increases until eventually he smashes all around him into ruin.
A man cannot live like a god, Odysseus is miserable on Calypso’s island, even though it is Greek Disneyland.
Too many programs, schools, and colleges are run as if our goal is to “do business.” This cannot be.
Instead, the goal of every ministry, school, or program must be to find our way to a home fit for men. That home cannot be some airy heaven, but must be middle earth where we were created to dwell.
Every task we do must be homeward bound. We create images of home here, so that we can find our eternal home tomorrow.
